The inference about the order did not come with it: no finding is made that EO 122 was timed for the forum, consistent with yesterday's page-by-page reading of the certified order, which names neither Pax Silica nor the United States. A sequence of dates is not a causal link. The finding-level gate cleared the new row only after striking two of its formulations. It refused the drafter's flat assertion that 'the proposed hub sits within the LEC' — true elsewhere in this report, but not something the USTDA notice establishes — and refused 'the agenda and speakers were not retrieved', which is imprecise where those pages are reachable and simply carry nothing yet. It also warned against implying that official material is silent on Clark, since the announcement names Clark among the locations to be visited. The published row states both things and does not collapse them. Three other candidates were gated today and all three were refused, which is why they are absent rather than present. A report of remarks by the US Senior Official to APEC on Pax Silica failed because no US-government transcript or readout substantiating the quotations was reachable. A report headlined that more than 700 indigenous people may be affected failed because the figure of '73 families or more than 700 individuals' appears only in the outlet's own narration and not in any quotation it attributes to the NCIP chairperson, no other outlet carries it, and it reconciles with none of the non-comparable estimates already on this record. No count changes, and the report's finding that no current, published, parcel-specific enumeration has been identified is unchanged. The third refusal is the one worth reading. A national daily attributed to a University of the Philippines discussion paper the warning that the Pax Silica site at New Clark City risks repeating the Bataan export-zone outcome. The gate refuted the attribution; the paper was then retrieved and read directly, and it confirms the refutation rather than overturning it. The passage warning that the project 'risks repeating history and becoming yet another primarily logistics-oriented initiative' is about the Luzon Economic Corridor, and Pax Silica appears in the paper only in a footnote. Nothing from that report enters this document. No Key Judgment, confidence level, scenario weight, precondition or red line moves, and no published number changes.

entries.title: The critical-minerals executive order is no longer a report about an instrument — the certified text is in hand
entries.summary: Since 24 August this report has carried Executive Order No. 122 as reporting rather than as an instrument, saying plainly that it had not located or authenticated the order's operative text. It has now been located. A certified copy — seven pages, stamped by the Malacañan Records Office on 19 August 2026 — was retrieved from the Official Gazette's own government domain on 28 August and read page by page. The reason four days of searching had failed is worth stating, because it is a trap anyone could fall into: the Gazette's website returns a security challenge on every ordinary article and section page, but serves the document itself directly from its downloads path. Reading the text confirms most of what had been reported and corrects three things this report had published. It also settles a narrower question: across all sixteen sections the order imposes no export prohibition, quota, levy or licensing requirement on mineral ore — so the comparison this report draws with Indonesia's nickel policy is no longer conditional on an unseen text, though it remains conditional on commodity coverage, on market position, and on the supplemental guidelines the order expressly leaves to be written. Two things we are not doing. We are not treating the order's silence as a record that the government considered and rejected an export restriction; silence in an instrument is not a decision. And we are not letting a mining order that never mentions Pax Silica, the United States or New Clark City move any judgment about the project — the adversarial gate called that analytical laundering, and it was right. No Key Judgment, confidence level, scenario weight, precondition or red line moves.

entries.title: The executive order was signed on 18 August, not 21 August — and the discrepancy is recorded rather than explained away
entries.supersedes: 21 Aug 2026 (reported signing date)
entries.summary: The order's execution clause reads: DONE, in the City of Manila, this 18th day of August. The timeline row is re-dated accordingly, and labelled an execution date rather than a publication or effectivity date, because those are different things and the order takes effect from publication. But 21 August was not a press invention, and it would be wrong to present it as one: the Department of Finance's own release also gives 21 August, as do Philstar and the Inquirer, while the Philippine News Agency gives 18 August. Whether 21 August marks an approval, a release or an error that propagated between outlets and departments is not established. We record the conflict and do not guess at it.

entries.title: The order's title was not what we published, and the word we quoted is the broadcaster's
entries.supersedes: Unified National Policy Framework for Developing the Critical Minerals Industry
entries.summary: The order's own caption reads: Establishing a National Policy Framework for Developing the Critical Minerals Industry and Reorganizing the Mining Industry Coordinating Council for the Purpose. There is no word Unified in it — that came from the government broadcaster's summary, and it is now attributed there. The second half of the title, the reorganisation of the Mining Industry Coordinating Council, we had omitted altogether, and it matters: the reorganised council now seats the Chairperson of the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples among its members. That is institutional representation and nothing more. It establishes nothing about whether free, prior and informed consent is required, obtained or adequate for anything at New Clark City, and the report says so in terms.

entries.title: There is no six-month cap on mining permit processing — the account we repeated was wrong
entries.supersedes: a maximum six-month permit-processing period
entries.summary: This report carried a secondary account describing a six-month maximum for processing mining permits. The text sets no such limit. What Section 7 actually does is give the mines bureau six months from the order's effectivity to put streamlined procedures in place — replacing sequential processing with simultaneous processing, setting timelines, and standing up an inter-agency monitoring committee — and one year to build an integrated digital platform consolidating national and local permits. Neither is a ceiling on how long any individual application may take, and neither is a limit on public consultation. The distinction matters because a processing cap and a deadline to reform processing are very different assurances.

entries.title: The verification date in the prefatory note had drifted a day behind the header and footer again
entries.supersedes: verified to 26 August 2026 and move forward as material developments are verified.
entries.summary: The note on timing at the head of this report said project facts were verified to 26 August while the page header and footer said 27 August. The header and footer were right; the note was not advanced with them when yesterday's revision shipped. All three now read 28 August. This is the fourth time this particular drift has occurred, and it is recorded here rather than quietly fixed because a page that asserts two different currency dates gives the reader no way to know which one to trust.

entries.title: The environment department exchange is no longer a single outlet's account — and the second account says more than the first
entries.supersedes: The exchange therefore rests on one outlet's account and is attributed to it throughout.
entries.summary: Yesterday we published the 26 August budget-hearing exchange with an explicit warning attached: it rested on GMA News Online's account alone. That warning is withdrawn, because it is no longer true. The Philippine Daily Inquirer and Radyo Pilipinas, the state broadcaster, published their own accounts of the same hearing on the same day, and the Manila Bulletin carried the environment bureau's position in summary form within its report. Secretary Cuna's quoted words are materially the same in GMA's account and the Inquirer's. Nothing published under the warning turned out to be wrong; what changes is that we no longer have to say it might be. The Inquirer adds three things GMA did not carry, each attributed to Environmental Management Bureau Director Michael Drake Matias. First, on the certificate: it was issued to BCDA for its master plan of the whole estate, which the Inquirer reports as “9,400 hectares”, with commercial, residential and open-park zoning marked in it. We carry that as a rounded press figure. The certificate's own text says 9,450.00 hectares under four titles, and the document controls. Second, on the parcel: BCDA's master plan for the roughly 1,600 hectares reportedly meant for Pax Silica indicated no specific project, and should one be indicated there, another impact assessment will be conducted. That is a statement of expectation, not evidence that any application will be filed or approved. Third, on locators: “wala pa rin pong malinaw na locators kung sino ang pupwesto doon… puro intent pa lang po din ang nakukuha ni BCDA from other potential locators” — no clear locators, expressions of intent only, on the information BCDA had given the regulator. That last one is the regulator relaying what the proponent told it, not an audit of anyone's commitments, and adversarial verification refused to let us use it to move the implementation scorecard. We have not moved it. A second official's name also enters, and we do not resolve which of them spoke. Radyo Pilipinas attributes the no-application statement to Environmental Management Bureau Region 3 Regional Director Martin Jose Despi rather than to Matias; the Manila Bulletin names no one. Both accounts can be true, since two officials may have spoken. Verification found Despi's regional post corroborated in the bureau's own regional records, while the records we located place Matias with the bureau's National Capital Region office rather than in a national directorship. We record the discrepancy and resolve nothing. Retrieving and transcribing the archived House recording would settle it, and we still have not done it. The water section gains the first defence of the water requirement to come from the legislature. Representative Jose “Pepito” Alvarez, who presided as vice chair and who also chairs the energy committee, told the hearing that the reported 60 million litres a day should not alarm anyone, because combining the discharge of all Zambales rivers into the ocean “every second is equivalent to that 60 million liters… only 60,000 cubic meters, which is one Panamax”. The conversion is correct and nothing else is. It sets a daily demand against an instantaneous flow; 60,000 cubic metres a second is an order of magnitude no Philippine river system approaches, and no supporting data was offered to the hearing or published afterwards; and the rivers are the wrong ones, since New Clark City sits in Capas, Tarlac and drains the Sacobia-Bamban system, while the Zambales rivers drain the other side of the range into the South China Sea. Panamax is a class of ship. The 60 million litre figure is also below BCDA's own published range of 65 to 90 million. Kabataan Representative Renee Co replied that the concerns are not confined to water but extend to power and land. We record the exchange as advocacy and evidence of the state of the argument, not as evidence about the water. Nothing in the catchment arithmetic changes. No key judgment, confidence level, scenario weight, precondition or red line moves; the verification pass was asked to challenge that and agreed with it.

entries.title: The New Clark City environmental compliance certificate is obtained — and it corrects two things this assessment had published
entries.supersedes: But the estate far exceeds the 25-hectare Category B threshold for industrial parks under EMB MC 2014-005 §3.6.6, so it unambiguously requires an ECC with a full EIS. None is on the public record, and no cumulative impact assessment exists.
entries.summary: The Bases Conversion and Development Authority has published, inside its own National Academy of Sports bidding documents, the environmental compliance certificate its president described at the Palace on 23 July 2026. We obtained it and read it in full. It is ECC-OL-R03-2019-0304, issued on 24 June 2019 by the Environmental Management Bureau Regional Office III in San Fernando, Pampanga, to BCDA, for the “proposed New Clark City Land Development Project” in Bamban and Capas, Tarlac, covering 9,450.00 hectares under four transfer certificates of title. It corrects this assessment in two places. First, the date: we had dated the certificate to 2017, following BCDA's president, and our source appendix gave “~2016–2018”. It is dated 24 June 2019, and that earlier dating is withdrawn. Whether BCDA's president was describing this certificate or another instrument associated with the 2017 master-plan process is not established, and we located no separate 2017 certificate. Second, and this one cuts against our own argument: we had said the estate “unambiguously requires an ECC with a full EIS” under item 3.6.6 of Environmental Management Bureau Memorandum Circular 2014-005, and that none was on the public record. Reading page 26 of that circular directly, item 3.6.5 — the classification on the face of the certificate — is not a non-industrial land-development category at all. It is “Industrial Parks (horizontal development) with critical slopes”, requiring an environmental impact statement at five hectares and above. The bureau classified the project under 3.6.5 and issued the certificate after a statement was submitted. Our assertion that New Clark City had no statement-backed zone-level certificate is therefore wrong, and it is withdrawn. What does not follow, and we say so expressly: a screening code is not proof of assessed scope. The project scope on the face of the certificate is its enumerated land-development components — administrative building, security offices, open spaces, utilities, housing, roads, transport hub and terminals, government institutional and warehouse facilities, emergency response facilities, perimeter fencing and gated entrance. No manufacturing, semiconductor, wafer-fabrication, data-centre or mineral-processing component is named. Restriction 25 of its Annex A subjects “any expansion or modification of the approved project components” to new environmental impact assessment requirements and requires individual locators to secure individual certificates before development. The certificate states that it “does not create any right nor be used as an authorization to implement the project”. Whether Pax Silica is such a modification, and whether the announced parcel lies within the certificate's boundary, are questions for the bureau; we assert neither in either direction, and we did not determine whether the certificate remains valid. Four adversarial verification passes were run against this text and three refused it. The first destroyed our central reasoning — we had proposed reading 3.6.5 as a land-development category contrasted with an industrial-estate 3.6.6, which is the opposite of what the circular says — and we then obtained the circular and confirmed the refusal against ourselves. The second caught the over-correction that followed, refusing to let a screening code stand in for assessed scope. The third struck an expiry insinuation the record did not support and required us to check the official House record before relying on a single news outlet, which we then did.

entries.title: The environment department says no Pax Silica impact assessment has been applied for, and no clear project description has reached it
entries.summary: GMA News Online reported that at the House appropriations committee briefing on the environment department's proposed ₱28.041-billion 2027 budget on 26 August 2026, Environment Secretary Juan Miguel T. Cuna, asked by Kabataan Party-list Representative Renee Louise Co whether an environmental impact assessment had been completed for Pax Silica, said: “There's been no environmental impact assessment applied for or processed this time. In fact, there's no clear project description actually that we are aware of at this time. For us to be able to intelligently assess any environmental impact, the project description should be clear. But as of now, there's been none that has been submitted to the EMB.” Of the site he said “yung 1,600 hectares, wala pa pong specific projects that will be allocated doon sa area”. Michael Drake P. Matias, identified by GMA News as Environmental Management Bureau Director, said a certificate had been issued for BCDA's development plan. We checked the official record. The House committee schedule places the briefing at 11 a.m. that day in Andaya Hall, to be livestreamed. The House's own published account of the hearing confirms the committee, its chair, that Palawan Representative Jose Alvarez presided as vice chair, that Cuna presented, and the budget figure — but it does not mention Pax Silica, an impact assessment, a certificate, or any exchange with Representative Co. That account is a selective summary, not a transcript, and we draw no inference from its silence: the omission neither contradicts nor corroborates GMA's account. We located an archived video entry for the hearing on the House video-streamings page and did not retrieve or transcribe it. The exchange therefore rests on one outlet's account and is attributed to it throughout. It strengthens the narrower finding this assessment has carried: as at 26 August 2026 no specifically described Pax Silica impact assessment application, and no clear project description, had reached the regulator that would have to receive one. The stakeholder map also gains the Anti-Red Tape Authority, which said in a statement reported on 25 and 26 August that it is working to reduce processing times and inter-agency bottlenecks for the project while insisting that streamlining “does not authorize the disregard for statutory mandates”. Four outlets carried it; they appear to be four renderings of one press statement rather than four independent sources, and the entry says so. The authority's own release was not reachable.

entries.title: The 24 August House budget hearing enters the activity-taxonomy section — and so does the hyperscale locator in BCDA's own bidder information
entries.summary: At the House appropriations committee hearing on the trade department's 2027 budget on 24 August 2026, Trade Undersecretary and Board of Investments Vice Chairman and Managing Head Ceferino S. Rodolfo told lawmakers that New Clark City “is just one of the projects, and it will be focused on advanced manufacturing” and that “the whole stack of AI, we will still discuss to determine other locations for those other areas” (Manila Bulletin). Pressed by ACT Teachers Representative Antonio Tinio, he said “what's clear is, in Clark, there is no data center”; answering Akbayan Representative Percival Cendaña, he said data centres “may happen in another location” where water and electricity are more available; and he disclosed talks “just last week” with an unidentified Metro Manila local government about a national integrated-circuit design hub, with a Pax Silica partner that is not the United States (Inquirer). ABS-CBN renders the exclusion as “the AI data centers themselves will not be in New Clark City”. Asked whether the electricity, water and environmental concerns are valid, he answered “yes, that is why we are taking inputs from everyone”. We did not retrieve an official transcript or archived recording of the hearing, although the House's own schedule records it and says it was to be livestreamed, so every quotation is carried as its outlet's account and not as authenticated testimony. Set beside that, the section now records where the assurance stops. Inside the site, officials have described small own-use facilities as possible: on 7 August the BCDA president said data centres established “if ever” would serve the semiconductor firms locating there, “not hyperscalers or major data centers that cater to global clients”, and the state news agency reported on 11 August, attributing unnamed trade officials, that there would be no major data centres “but small ones that will be operated by the locators or the manufacturers for their own use”. Outside it, BCDA's own July 2025 bidder information for the New Clark City ICT corridor — Annex F to Bid Bulletin No. 5 — lists among the city's industrial locators a “Hyperscale Data Center” of 47.0 hectares, with construction stated to start in the fourth quarter of 2025. The state news agency reported the underlying transaction in June 2024: a lease contract agreement signed alongside the Tarlac governor for a 47-hectare New Clark City site, for a 300-megawatt hyperscale facility in three 100-megawatt phases at about 890 million US dollars each, 2.7 billion in total. We found no authoritative 2026 confirmation of that project's construction, schedule, cancellation or current status, and nothing we located establishes whether its parcel lies inside or outside the proposed Pax Silica parcel. We draw no inference either way. Five adversarial gate passes refused four earlier drafts of this material. The gate struck our claim that this was the first data-centre exclusion by an agency other than BCDA — Rodolfo had said substantially the same at the Senate environment committee on 14 August, which we already record; our word “relocates”, because the record supports only “may happen in another location”; our description of a planned “economic zone”, because what is reported is a prospective industrial hub; and our characterisation of the proponents' position as internally coherent, because the 24 August formulations drop the own-use exception the 7 August statement had made. It also caught our citation of the BCDA annex as Annex E when it is Annex F, required us to flag rather than silently repair the state news agency's printed “4-acre” figure for what is a 4,000-acre parcel, and required us to carry rather than resolve the 47-, 50- and 52-hectare discrepancy between BCDA's 2020 account of the Tarlac allocation and the 2024 report. All of those repairs are in the published text. The finding is unchanged and is not weakened: the formally adopted activity mix of the proposed parcel remains undeclared. The assurance has become more categorical without becoming more precisely defined or internally consistent, and no instrument we located sets the line between a permissible own-use facility and an excluded major one, names who draws it, or says what happens if a locator's facility grows past it. No Key Judgment, confidence level, scenario weight, precondition or red line moves. One claim-checker row is added, with its paired attribution row. The date to which project facts are verified advances to 25 August 2026.

entries.title: A reported critical-minerals executive order enters the record — as reporting, not as an instrument — and the site's own hearing-era name enters the entity list
entries.summary: Two additions today, and both were rewritten by the adversarial gate before publication. First, Executive Order No. 122, series of 2026, reported as signed on 21 August 2026, establishing what the government broadcaster PTV describes as a Unified National Policy Framework for Developing the Critical Minerals Industry and reorganising the Mining Industry Coordinating Council under the environment and finance secretaries as co-chairs. We did not locate or authenticate the order's operative text: it was not in the Official Gazette index, which ended at Executive Order 121 of 29 July 2026, nor in the Lawphil index, nor on any Presidential Communications Office, environment department or Mines and Geosciences Bureau page we could reach, as checked on 24 August 2026. That records the limits of our searches and is not proof of non-publication. The timeline and section 15.1.1 therefore describe reporting about the order rather than verified provisions of it. The gate refused both of our drafts outright, holding that they turned descriptions of an unavailable instrument into findings about what it contains or omits. It struck our line that the order imposes no restriction on mineral ore export, because a report that exports remain permitted does not exclude a qualification, an exception, a delegation or a later implementing rule. It struck our conclusion that this was the regulatory lever our Indonesia comparator identified, pulled short of the notch that mattered, because that converts silence in incomplete summaries into a finding that the government affirmatively declined an export restriction; the Indonesia comparison is published conditionally instead. It required that criticism from Representative Antonio Tinio and from AGHAM's Giovanni Tapang be carried as attributed reaction with its reporting chain named, because no primary statement from either was located. No source we reviewed reports that the order mentions Pax Silica, the United States or New Clark City; the connection is drawn by the reporting and by critics, not by the order. Second, the entity list gains the name Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park, which the proponents used at the Senate committee hearing of 14 August 2026 and which this assessment had not carried for ten days. That gate also refused our draft, striking the categorical claim that the proponents' own name for the Philippine site is therefore not Pax Silica: the Filipino sentence carrying it is the reporter's narrative voice rather than a quotation of Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo, its pronoun has no stated antecedent, and the same article's headline calls the project Pax Silica. The name is published as reported, hearing-era and provisional, distinguished from the designations that appear in instruments. A separate report that officials were considering dropping the Pax Silica label was gated and refused as an unattributed inference no other account supports, and is not published. No Key Judgment, confidence level, scenario weight or precondition moves. Key Judgment 12 gains an evidence pointer only, on the gate's express instruction that its judgment and confidence be retained and revisited when an authenticated text and implementing rules become available.

entries.title: A stale verification date in the prefatory note is corrected
entries.supersedes: This is a living document. Project facts are verified to 15 August 2026 and move forward as material developments are verified.
entries.summary: The prefatory note on timing and currency carried 15 August 2026 as the date to which project facts are verified, while the page header and footer carried 23 August. The header and footer were right and the prefatory note had not been moved forward with them, so for nine days the page asserted two different verification dates. The note now reads 24 August 2026, in step with every other surface. This is a surface-drift correction: no finding, date of verification or conclusion changes because of it, and the superseded sentence is quoted above so the drift can be checked rather than taken on trust.

entries.title: An NCIP census announcement, refused yesterday as single-source, is admitted today as an announcement — and moves nothing
entries.summary: Version 2.34 refused a Daily Tribune report that the NCIP had conducted a census of Aeta Hungey households at Sitio Sapang Kawayan, because only one carrier and no underlying NCIP statement had then been located. That refusal was correct on the record then available, and meant insufficient corroboration rather than disproof. Today's sweep surfaced the story through a second channel, and retrieval of the full Daily Tribune text together with a Rappler Communities post by reporter Paolo Cootauco of 22 August established what yesterday's run did not have: the underlying source is an NCIP social-media announcement dated 20 August 2026, quoted by Rappler verbatim in Filipino, expressly credited by News5, and carried also by Brigada Balita and NET25. The proposition therefore changed. Yesterday we were asked to accept on one outlet's word that a census occurred; today we record only that the commission announced the activity. The announcement is multiply evidenced; the underlying activity is not independently corroborated, and we say so. The additional carriers appear substantially derivative and none of the reports examined claims independent on-site observation. Section 15.2.1 gains two paragraphs and the timeline a row for 20 to 21 August, the activity date left unresolved on the page because the reports cite an NCIP post dated 20 August while News5 described the visit as occurring on Friday 21 August. The Daily Tribune named NCIP Ethnographic Commissioner for Region III and the Rest of Luzon Rhodex Valenciano, NCIP Region III Director Joyce Lapuz and Aeta Hungey Chieftain Petronila Capiz-Munoz among those present, and reported the commission as saying the exercise seeks an accurate and complete record of the indigenous cultural communities in the area. No household, family or person total resulting from the activity has been identified, so none of the figures already before the Senate is displaced or confirmed, and no boundary, method or reference date is public. Nothing published identifies the activity as a Section 59 field-based investigation, a Certification Precondition process or an FPIC proceeding, and nothing published places it outside those processes either; its procedural status is undisclosed, so our finding that the certification precondition process shows no sign of having been initiated is untouched. The adversarial gate refused our first draft outright and the published wording is largely the gate's own. It struck the claim that the commission had moved from dialogue to enumeration, because the 8 August dialogue was at Sitio Binyayan and this activity at Sitio Sapang Kawayan and no progression between procedural stages is established; it struck 'no figure of any kind has been released' as too absolute; it struck 'each report traces to the same NCIP announcement and none reports independent on-site observation' as exceeding what was shown; it struck 'NCIP's own website carries nothing' as broader than a site search can support; it struck a reference to the parcel finally leased, no lease existing; and it struck our claim that publishing the census would be the cheapest de-risking step available to the commission, because the report already reserves that description for the Section 59 certification precondition process, which publication would neither establish nor substitute for. No Key Judgment, confidence level, scenario weight or precondition moves. Displacement stays Disputed.

entries.title: The enumeration finding's search date advances to 23 August, on a fresh search rather than on the census report
entries.summary: Section 15.2.1's operative finding — that no current, published, parcel-specific enumeration reporting households and persons on a common reference date has been identified — moves from 'as at 20 August 2026' to 'as at 23 August 2026'. Version 2.34 expressly declined to advance that date because its source had not passed the gate. The basis for advancing it today is different and independent of the census report: a fresh negative search made on 23 August. NCIP's own website was re-checked, where a site search for 'Pax Silica' returns no result and the News and Events listing shows no item later than 14 August 2026, and a separate search for any published result of the reported census was also negative. The gate ruled expressly that the date may advance on that search and not on the strength of the activity announcement, which publishes no result and therefore neither advances nor prevents advancing it. The wording distinguishing the two grounds is published on the page so the basis can be checked rather than taken on trust. 'Project facts verified to' advances to 23 August 2026. No finding, Key Judgment, confidence level, scenario weight or precondition moves.

entries.title: Akbayan's demand for a congressional inquiry enters the record as House Resolution 1227
entries.summary: Until now this report named only one numbered congressional instrument on Pax Silica, the Makabayan bloc's House Resolution 1128 of 19 June 2026, and recorded Akbayan's parallel demand as an unformalised urging. The House of Representatives' own legislative record establishes that Akbayan party-list Representatives Perci Cendana, Chel Diokno and Dadah Kiram Ismula, together with Dinagat Islands Lone District Representative Kaka Bag-ao, filed House Resolution 1227 on 28 July 2026 — a resolution urging the appropriate House committees to conduct an inquiry, in aid of legislation, into the Pax Silica Initiative, particularly its projected economic benefits, environmental, labor, social, and national security implications, and the adequacy of existing laws and regulations governing its implementation. The House read it on 3 August and referred it to the Committee on Economic Affairs, where it has been pending since 11 August 2026. The timeline, the opposition-coalition passage, the stakeholder map's Akbayan entry and the source appendix are updated together. Filing and referral establish no inquiry: none has been calendared, heard or reported out, and we say so in terms. The adversarial gate refused our first draft and the published wording is the gate's own. It caught a filing date of 29 July that we had taken from press reporting where the House record says 28 July; it held that the resolution's granular demands — foregone revenues, the terms of the land lease including the two-year rent-free period, a Fiscal Incentives Review Board review of incentive redundancy, and the projected demand for and cost allocation of electricity, water, transport, telecommunications and digital infrastructure — rest on a single reporter's copy, cannot be checked against the filed text, and largely restate what we already record, so they are not published; and it refused an imported unit error, the description of the affected land as 4,000 hectares, where the site is approximately 4,000 acres, about 1,618.74 hectares. The filed text of HR 1227 was not retrievable and is recorded among the documents we have not obtained. Two other items from the same day's sweep were gated and refused, and are not published. A report that the NCIP conducted a census of Aeta Hungey households at Sitio Sapang Kawayan on 21 August was refused as single-source; the gate noted that this means insufficient corroboration rather than disproof, and established that the report publishes no household total, person total, reference date or mapped coverage in any event, so our finding that no published parcel-specific enumeration has been identified is untouched and its date is not advanced. And a "200,000 direct jobs" figure circulating this week was traced to press rounding of BCDA's existing 190,000 upper bound from the briefings of 23 to 27 July, not a new official claim, so our count of five distinct official employment figures is unchanged. No Key Judgment, confidence level, scenario weight or precondition moves.

entries.title: The State Department's signatory roster has been updated, and our description of it is corrected
entries.supersedes: the State Department’s own Pax Silica page lists 23 signatories and omits the United States from its own roster, so counting the page yields 23
entries.summary: This site described the State Department's Pax Silica page in the present tense as listing 23 signatories, and used that to explain why President Marcos called the initiative "23-member strong" in the State of the Nation Address of 27 July 2026. Fetched directly on 21 August 2026, the page's Signatories section now lists 24 entries — Italy among them, added after its accession to the Declaration at Brindisi on 31 July — and still omits the United States from its own roster. Counting the page therefore now yields 24 against a standing signatory count of 25. The superseded sentence is quoted above and rewritten in the past tense, anchored to 27 July, which remains accurate for that date. The substance of the finding is unchanged and is not weakened: the defect it identifies is the omission of the United States from the initiative's own published roster, and that omission survives the update. We claim only that the page read as described on the date we fetched it; a current page cannot establish its own former contents, and the earlier roster rests on our dated enumeration of 26 June 2026. The standing count remains 25.

entries.title: BCDA's president puts the first phase at around 500 hectares on a three-to-five-year horizon
entries.summary: At a New Clark City briefing on 7 August 2026, BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang said: "We see this as a long-term (investment). The first phase will be around 500 hectares. We see that in three to five years." The Philippine News Agency headlined and led on this as site development "eyed to start" within three to five years, and PTV News carried the report the following day. We record the quotation and the agency's interpretation of it as separate things, because the quoted words do not specify whether the period runs to the commencement or the delivery of the first phase, and because "site development" is not established to be the same milestone as the "construction" of BCDA's indicative schedule of 23 July 2026. It is therefore recorded as an official statement that introduces ambiguity, not as a schedule that displaces the early-2028 construction indication against which this report tests other claims. A drafted reading that the horizon showed the schedule slipping to 2029–2031 was refused by the verification gate and is not published. No official reconciliation of the two formulations was identified in the sources searched to 21 August 2026. Separately, the first phase's extent is now stated inconsistently: the Senate record of 14 August describes an approximately 580-hectare first phase, against Bingcang's "around 500 hectares". Both are approximate and the record does not establish a shared boundary, scope or reference date, so the variation is recorded and not resolved.

entries.title: BCDA publicly qualifies its own November signing target, and rules out hyperscale data centres
entries.summary: On 19 August 2026 BusinessWorld and GMA News reported BCDA President and CEO Joshua M. Bingcang saying the agency was still aiming to sign the framework agreement by November but that "negotiations can always take longer" — BusinessWorld rendering his description of the target as "not set in stone", GMA News as "not cast in stone". The claim checker's framework row is rewritten around that qualification, and its verdict moves from an official projection to an official target that the proponent has publicly described as subject to negotiation and possible delay. The two reports carry the same remarks by the same official on the same day and are recorded on the page as not independent corroboration; the outlets name the forum differently, so this report asserts no venue, and no transcript or recording was located to resolve the wording. A new §12.2.6 in the assessment records that BusinessWorld reported Bingcang saying the hub is "purely commercial", will have no defence-related activities, and that no hyperscale data centres would be built for it, and that the Inquirer separately reported him linking this to New Clark City's current power infrastructure. Those reports are consistent with a material existing-infrastructure constraint but establish none of KJ-8's separate conclusions about the approximately 3 GW estimate, on-site or near-site solar, or the absence of a published supply plan; the accompanying assurance of an "embedded, independent power supply" is the same conditional assurance already graded, and a goal is not commissioned capacity. Also recorded: the Philippine News Agency's published description changed between 19 June, when hyperscale data centres appeared among the facilities expected at the development in the agency's own descriptive wording, and 7 August, when it reported Bingcang excluding hyperscalers. The report records the change in the published description and does not assert that the underlying official position changed. No key judgment, confidence level, scenario weight or precondition moves.

entries.title: The reading that the clearest population discrepancy lies between BCDA and NCIP is withdrawn
entries.supersedes: The clearest reported discrepancy is therefore between BCDA's lower household estimate and NCIP's 75-household figure
entries.summary: ABS-CBN reported on 18 August 2026 that NCIP Chairperson Nancy Catamco said at the 14 August Senate hearing that the chieftain had initially reported the 75 households or families. If that is accurate, the 75-household figure may not be independent of the community evidence behind the figure of about 1,000 people, and this report's framing — which treated it as an independent NCIP estimate against BCDA's lower count — does not hold. The sentence is withdrawn from the running text; it is quoted verbatim above, which is where this project keeps retired text. The report does not conclude the opposite: it does not treat the two community-associated figures as comparable, because the available reporting establishes no common reference date, geographic scope, population definition or counting unit, and "households or families" is itself ambiguous. The operative finding is unchanged and restated with its limits: as at 20 August 2026 no current, published, parcel-specific enumeration reporting households and persons on a common reference date has been identified, and until one is, none of the reported figures can be treated as independently verified. The adversarial gate deleted the drafter's supporting arithmetic entirely — 75 households against about 1,000 people implies roughly thirteen people per household — as analytically unsound without a shared denominator, scope and reference date, and as insinuating exaggeration by a community from an invalid comparison. It is not published. Displacement stays disputed.

entries.title: The 2027 date in the framework-signature row referred to planning, not framework finalisation
entries.supersedes: Other statements point to 2027 finalisation; Finance Sec. Go says "within the year".
entries.summary: The claim checker's framework row carried 2027 as a competing framework-finalisation date. It was mis-scoped. The Presidential Communications Office release of 23 July 2026 places contract negotiations during 2026, planning in 2027 and construction beginning in early 2028 — an implementation schedule, not an alternative signing date. The sequence is not lost: it moves to the assessment's timeline at 23 July 2026 with its "expected" modality preserved. Finance Secretary Go's "I hope we can get something signed within the year" is retained and now carries its full attribution — 7 July 2026, reported by Manila Bulletin, which scopes the remark to the framework agreement for the hub, with Foxconn described separately as a possible anchor locator; no transcript was located, so the scope rests on the outlet's framing. That attribution was itself the subject of a refusal: the drafter proposed correcting the quote as mis-scoped to Foxconn, and the adversarial gate established from the source that it is not, so the drafter's proposed correction was withdrawn in full and nothing in the Foxconn row was touched.

entries.title: A water figure withdrawn as unsourceable has been located; it is still not adopted
entries.supersedes: a "130 MLD water figure" carried in the monitoring ledger since 29 July could not be sourced anywhere
entries.summary: Version 2.8 withdrew a 130 MLD water figure on the ground that it could not be sourced. The corpus-specific part of that finding stands — the figure was absent from this report and from the 6,437-row social-listening export examined — but the broader statement was too categorical. An Inquirer article bylined Dr. Teodoro Mendoza PhD, published 30 July 2026, states that the project "is expected to require about 130 million liters of water a day and 3 gigawatts of electricity, equivalent to 16% of Luzon's current grid capacity." Separately, Bilyonaryo News Channel reported on 19 August 2026 that Dr. Guillermo Q. Tabios III of the UP Institute of Civil Engineering and the UP National Hydraulic Research Center said "they were talking about 180 million liters per day that they would require" — the outlet's own paraphrase says the development "would require" it, but the direct quotation leaves the antecedent of "they" and the figure's origin unresolved, so this report does not treat it as Tabios's independent estimate. Neither figure is adopted: the sources examined provide no underlying calculation and do not specify project scope, development stage, process mix, recycling assumption or water-balance methodology. The assessment's water arithmetic continues to test BCDA's claim against BCDA's own disclosed 65 to 90 million litres per day, and does not change. Tabios's grid-share comparison is deliberately not reproduced, because it uses a denominator different from the peak-demand figures this report works from and the percentages are not comparable. The historical change-log entry is left unedited; this entry supersedes it.

entries.title: A departure date reported to residents at Sitio Sapang Kawayan, and the budget's silence on Pax Silica
entries.summary: Two additions from the Philippine domestic record. §15.2.1 gains the residents' own account, gathered on site by ABS-CBN and published 18 August 2026: Ralph Gelmar Lozano said he and other residents were told their houses would be affected and that they could be required to leave by December, and Antero Capiz separately recalled being told they had only until Christmas; residents said they had not been told where they would be relocated or what assistance would be provided, and that payment would cover their houses but apparently not the land; and Capiz said graves of relatives in Sitio Binyayan had already been bulldozed. That last point is in tension with BCDA's hearing statement that Binyayan would not be disturbed, and the report says so without resolving it — the reporting establishes neither when the earlier bulldozing occurred nor who carried it out, and Capiz described the graves nearer the present community as not yet disturbed. None of it is an agency record: no BCDA notice, valuation schedule, relocation plan or demolition order corresponding to a December date has been published, and none was located. Separately, the timeline gains 17 August 2026: at the House committee on appropriations hearing on the ₱7.2-trillion 2027 National Expenditure Program, DBM Secretary Kim Robert de Leon said the proposed NEP contains no allocation intended for Pax Silica, and DOF Secretary Frederick Go said the hub is "still under very preliminary discussion" and that "there's nothing in the budget that will spend for this proposed industrial hub because nothing has been signed" — recorded as limited fiscal corroboration of the pre-decisional finding, since hearing testimony is not a line-by-line examination of the NEP schedules. The claim checker gains one row: Go's statement that if a hub is built there is "no budget requirement from us" and "they will pay us rent", graded Projection, because the published instrument setting out the proposed land terms provides a two-year rent-free period and quantifies neither the Year-3 rent nor the lease term. The adversarial gate refused all three texts three times across four rounds before clearing them; its sharpest catch was that the drafter's note double-counted the Philippine concession, since the proposal identifies the rent-free period itself as the in-kind contribution rather than the land separately. No key judgment, confidence level or scenario weight moves: displacement stays Disputed.

entries.title: The claim-verification matrix holds fifty-two claims, not forty-nine
entries.supersedes: The claim-verification matrix: forty-nine claims adjudicated.
entries.summary: The section's own subtitle undercounted the matrix it introduces. The claim checker rendered fifty-one claims before today and fifty-two after the row added above; the subtitle had said forty-nine, a count left behind by earlier additions rather than an error at the time it was written. Found by the post-verification review while adding a claim, not by the day's candidates. Corrected on the site; the noscript digest carries the corrected figure through the crawler-text rebuild. Stated as a correction rather than edited away, on a page that grades other parties' arithmetic. The assessment's own §4 tables in the master document hold more rows than the site's curated matrix; that difference is by design and the two counts are not interchangeable.

entries.title: The no-displacement claim row still carried the attribution corrected in v2.26
entries.supersedes: ~1,000 people associated with the Sitio Sapang Kawayan chieftain
entries.summary: v2.26 established that the 14 August hearing recording does not identify who gave the figure of about 1,000 people, and restated it as reported by a community witness describing Sitio Sapang Kawayan's own census. That correction reached §15.2.1 of the master document and the site's claim note, but not the summary row in §4.1, which carried the withdrawn attribution for four days. The row is aligned here and the miss is stated rather than edited away. Separately noted and deliberately not acted on: the 18 August ABS-CBN report attributes the census figure to the chieftain, Petronila Capiz-Munoz, by name. Restoring an attribution this report deliberately withdrew is a finding-level change and was not put to the adversarial gate today, so it stands unchanged pending one.

entries.title: Finding 05 restated on the one-scheme relabelled series
entries.supersedes: Across 6,437 mentions from December to SONA eve, net sentiment fell from −1.0 before accession to −24.8 after, and to −34.8 in July alone. The economics are argued both ways. Water, land and governance are not debated at all; they run at net −44, −50 and −54. The best sentiment month on record was May, when the government publicly refused a US request.
entries.summary: The finding card still summarised the public conversation in the sampled export's vendor labels — including a May best-month observation that does not survive the v2.30 relabelling — while the exhibit beside it showed the one-scheme series. The card now states the relabelled arc (clearly positive early months between +25 and +51 net, +5.3 in June, −35.6 in July), its key figure moves from −34.8 to the relabelled July value −35.6, and the topic figures are explicitly framed as the sampled export analysis. The finding itself — the public has already turned, and on the unanswered questions — is unchanged and is larger under the relabelled series. The vendor-labelled record remains in section 19 and §17A as the export analysis, per the v2.30 relabelling note; the superseded card text is quoted here verbatim.

entries.title: Volume estimate markers move from bar labels to tooltips and the chart note
entries.summary: The approximation signs on the sampled-period volume bars and the per-month ×10 tags on the axis are removed for readability, at the publisher's direction. The figures are unchanged and remain estimates: the chart note still states that bars before the seam are the sampled counts multiplied by ten, each bar's tooltip still names itself an estimate, and the day view's peak label says so when the peak is an estimated day.

entries.title: Sampled-period volumes now shown as ×10 universe estimates
entries.summary: The volume views previously charted the January–July period at its raw sample counts beside the near-complete August collection, which made the earlier conversation look a tenth of its real size. Those bars now multiply the sampled counts by ten — the provider's stated sampling rate, and the same universe-estimate framing section 19 has always used — marked with ≈ on every figure and named as estimates in the chart note and tooltips. A platform check this evening found the true monthly multiple ranges from about nine to about twelve, so these are deliberately rough estimates, not counts; the near-complete period remains actual collected counts, and sentiment shares are unaffected because shares never depended on the sampling rate. No basis or method changes elsewhere.

entries.title: The daily sentiment view is now a bar chart
entries.summary: The daily net-sentiment view drew a line that the honesty mask repeatedly broke — sparse weeks are deliberately blanked rather than guessed, and a line full of breaks read as fragments. It is now a bar chart: each bar is the same trailing seven-day average, diverging from the zero line and coloured like the monthly view, and masked days are simply blank. No figure or method changes.

entries.title: Day-view sentiment scale now fits the relabelled history; the exhibit's charts animate
entries.summary: A presentation defect, hours old: the daily net-sentiment line used a fixed vertical scale chosen before the relabelled history existed, and the strongly positive January–May weeks ran off the top of the chart. The scale is now computed from the data itself, padded and always including zero, so nothing can clip as the series grows. No figure changes. The exhibit's charts also gain motion — bars grow in, the daily line draws on, fills stagger — with animation disabled for readers who prefer reduced motion and in print, so the downloadable PDF always shows finished charts.

entries.title: One running listening exhibit replaces the two social-listening sections
entries.supersedes: A social listening export covering 6 December 2025 to 27 July 2026: a stated 10% sample of global public mentions, excluding reshares. The rate is the provider’s statement, not independently benchmarked, so shares here are sample-dependent estimates.
entries.summary: Exhibit 12 and the daily 'current listening' block were two views of one conversation, one frozen in late July and one moving, measured on different bases. They are now a single exhibit running from 1 January 2026 to the current date, refreshed daily by the same gated pipeline, with month and day views and the measurement seam drawn on the chart. Two changes are substance, not layout. First, the historical mentions from the sampled export were relabelled by the same local software that labels the current collection, so sentiment, topics and speaker types use one scheme across the whole series; the vendor's labels remain unpublished. The relabelling confirms July's collapse almost exactly (net −35.6 against the export analysis's −34.8) but reads January–May as clearly positive toward the project where the earlier labels read near-neutral wire coverage — and the May recovery the report's section 19 describes does not appear under the new labels, which is stated in the assessment's v2.30 note rather than smoothed over. Second, the exhibit's headline figures and the hero tile now cover the near-complete collection that began 7 August 2026 rather than the mixed whole window, moving the displayed negative share from 48.2% to 46.0% and the hero net from −22.0 to −18.2 at the time of this release — a declared basis choice, not a data revision. Counts are still shown per basis, the uncollected 28 July–6 August days render as a gap, and finding 05 and section 19 keep the frozen July figures as the historical record of the sampled export. Assessment v2.30 documents the relabelling, its concordance with the vendor labels, and the review status of the decision in Appendix H.27.

entries.title: The hero's sentiment figure now tracks the daily listening data
entries.supersedes: −34.8 · net public sentiment in july, from −1.0 pre-accession
entries.summary: The page hero carried a July figure, net −34.8, drawn from the sampled listening export that section 19 analyses. It was typed by hand, so it did not move when the daily listening data moved. It now reports the same measurement the listening exhibit below it shows — net −21.6 across the 19,819 mentions the classifier labelled in the window ending 17 August — and it is generated from that snapshot by the script that renders the exhibit, inside a marked region nobody edits by hand. Two things follow. The two figures are not interchangeable: the retired one is July, on a sampled export carrying the data provider's own labels; the new one is the current window on this site's classifier, which is the only sentiment this site publishes. And the July finding does not change — finding 05 and section 19 still report net −34.8 for July, −24.8 after accession and −1.0 before it, because those remain accurate for the period and the method they describe. What the tile drops is the pre-accession comparison, which was only meaningful inside the export it came from. The new caption names its own denominator and does not describe the figure as a trend: the window is 249 days, but the mentions in it are not evenly spread across those days.

entries.title: The retired player's audio and scripts leave the server
entries.supersedes: The audio files the old player once played remain on the server unreferenced for now; removing served files is a separate decision because archived copies of old page versions may still point at them.
entries.summary: The decision deferred in the last entry is now taken, by the publisher. Removed from the server: the thirty-three audio clips of the original English explainer, the single-file Taglish narration that replaced them for three days in early August, the old player's standalone offline export, and the two narration-script files — about four point seven megabytes across thirty-seven files, none referenced by any served page since the video player arrived on 6 August. The crawl rules that blocked these paths from indexing go with them, since there is nothing left to block; the archive directory's rule stays. The script that checks the live deployment is updated in the same release: it no longer asserts these files are reachable, and now asserts the opposite — each removed path must return not-found on every future check, so a bad revert cannot quietly resurrect them. Readers who saved the page before 6 August and replay it offline will find its audio gone; the current explainer video is unaffected. The narration scripts and recordings remain preserved in the project's private archive, where the provenance record for this week's correction already cites them. No text, figure or finding changes.

entries.title: The retired player's code leaves the page
entries.summary: Housekeeping that follows this morning's correction. The page source still carried the whole engine of the pre-video explainer player — the caption and audio machinery retired when the video moved into its own frame — and one line of its leftover data is what yesterday's false disclosure was built on. The data was removed this morning; this release removes the rest: the player's methods, its scene table, its clip list, and the control wiring nothing references. About seven kilobytes of dead code, verified dead by reference analysis before removal — every removed piece had no path from anything the page renders. What the reader sees does not change. The explainer modal — auto-open, the watch button, fullscreen, close — was exercised in a browser against the trimmed page before publication, and behaves identically. The audio files the old player once played remain on the server unreferenced for now; removing served files is a separate decision because archived copies of old page versions may still point at them. No text, figure or finding changes.

entries.title: We said the deployed Taglish video still said fifteen. It did not.
entries.supersedes: "The explainer video's narration remains the one knowingly dated copy, as disclosed yesterday, pending its next recut." — and, from the entry of 16 August: "One surface is knowingly left as recorded: the explainer video's narration says fifteen, because that is what was recorded on 14 August; it will be corrected the next time the video is recut, and until then this entry is the notice of the discrepancy."
entries.summary: When this site corrected the gate count on 16 August, it disclosed one surface as knowingly left dated: the explainer video's narration, said to still say fifteen until the next recut. The publisher watched the video and pointed out that it says no such thing. He is right. The fifteen-line was recorded for the original English explainer, replaced on this site on 3 August; every later explainer narration identified in the deployment history — including the current 2:05 cut and its 14 August recut — states no gate count, in English or Filipino. A full machine transcription of the deployed video found no gate-count wording, corroborating the script and direct review of the video. There was nothing for a recut to fix. What still said fifteen was leftover data in the page's source code: the caption table of the retired player, which had no bound caption node, no playable audio source, and no markup control capable of activating it — and which we misread as the live narration when writing the disclosure. The video was right and the footnote about it was wrong — in the report's version note, in its appendix, and in both prior entries here. This release removes the stale caption data, removes the check exemption that treated captions as faithful copies of recorded audio — that assumption is precisely what failed — and extends the mechanical check to read the count in Filipino as well as English, with planted regressions; each change was verified against the release diff and test output before this entry was published. The correction does not change the master scorecard's tally of fourteen open gates of sixteen. The deployed narration states no count.

entries.title: The hero still said 15 of 16 — a fourth copy of the corrected count
entries.supersedes: { v: '15 / 16', k: 'implementation gates still open' }
entries.summary: Yesterday's correction of the implementation-gate count — fourteen open, not fifteen — reached the checklist, the section text, the metadata and the report, and was then checked mechanically. It missed one more copy: the large statistic on the front of the site, which kept saying 15 / 16 because it stores the number in a different shape — a tile with a numeral, not a sentence with a word — and the new mechanical check only knew how to read sentences. A reader caught it within a day. The tile now says 14 / 16, and the check has been taught the numeric form, with a test that plants the old tile and confirms publication would be refused. The lesson is the same one this changelog keeps recording, one surface later each time: a fact published in four formats is four chances to miss one, and every format needs its own guard. The explainer video's narration remains the one knowingly dated copy, as disclosed yesterday, pending its next recut.

entries.title: The implementation checklist: fourteen gates open, not fifteen
entries.supersedes: Fifteen of sixteen gates are open.
entries.summary: This report has said, since its first edition on 27 July, that fifteen of the sixteen implementation gates are open. Its own checklist has said otherwise the whole time. The scorecard in section 10 closes two gates — the political declaration signed on 16 April, and the land offer made on 9 April — and the section's own heading counts both: one political declaration, one unilateral offer. Two closed means fourteen open. The sentence under the table, and Key Judgment 16, said fifteen: an arithmetic slip at authoring that propagated to the site's checklist heading, its section text, its machine-readable metadata, and the narration of the explainer video, and survived twenty-seven releases because nothing compared the claim to the checklist it describes. A reader prompted the check that found it. Nothing about the project has changed: no gate opened or closed this week, the judgment that the project is pre-decisional stands at unchanged confidence, and BCDA's own FOI denial — which confirmed the planning-stage status, not any particular count — is unaffected. The checklist's note on the land offer now also records what version 2.24 established: the United States accepted the offer conditionally in principle on 16 April, and nothing is executed. One surface is knowingly left as recorded: the explainer video's narration says fifteen, because that is what was recorded on 14 August; it will be corrected the next time the video is recut, and until then this entry is the notice of the discrepancy. From this release, the count shown is checked mechanically against the checklist itself on every publication.

entries.title: We put the funding notice on the news rail on 13 August and left the report saying it was still planned
entries.summary: The routine review that follows every verified finding turned up a fault of our own before it turned up anything about Pax Silica. On 13 August we verified and published, on this site's news rail, the State Department's notice launching the Pax Silica AI Assistance Project. The section of the report that lists what the initiative has actually delivered went on calling that same notice *planned* for three more days. Two parts of one document disagreeing, in public, about a fact we had already checked. It is corrected here and stated as a correction. Two things our rail item said are restated at the same time: the fifty million dollars is the register's ceiling for a single award, not a programme total — the total field is blank — and the posted notice's public summary does not mention Panama, which came from earlier reporting. What the notice is: the Pax Silica Artificial Intelligence Assistance Project, number DFOP0019193, from the State Department's Bureau of Economic and Business Affairs, listed under Economic Statecraft. State listed it on 12 August; the register shows a version 2 posted 14 August and applications closing 20 August. A cooperative agreement, three expected awards between one and fifty million dollars, open only to for-profit organisations other than small businesses, for a trusted supply-chain credentialing platform and something it calls a Silicon Highway — a digital-physical corridor with cryptographic cargo verification. It says it draws on foreign assistance from a Pax Fund, a name for which we could find no published authority, appropriation or size. The scale is the point: a solicitation is not a financing facility, no award has been made, and one to fifty million dollars is three to five orders of magnitude below the forty to seventy billion the New Clark City project is marketed at. Separately, and moving no judgement: Reuters reported — carried by CNBC on 15 August and by GMA in Manila on 16 August — that the State Department has drafted a letter to the 35 signatories of the Joint Statement on AI Opportunity, the Philippines among them, warning they will be excluded from Pax Silica if they also join a competing framework, and telling them signature 'cannot be held alongside membership in duplicative initiatives'. The draft is undated and unsent, Reuters could not establish when or whether it would go out, the State Department declined to comment on purportedly leaked internal documents, and the story rests on one news organisation and one anonymous official; the many republications are the same wire copy, not corroboration. The verification pass refused both our drafts twice before clearing them — it struck an eight-day application window we had invented, cut 'first money' back to what the evidence supports, fixed our order-of-magnitude arithmetic, corrected the Reuters date, and made us attribute three quoted phrases to the Declaration rather than to both instruments.
entries.supersedes: a planned funding opportunity for an AI supply-chain provenance platform piloted in Panama

entries.title: We said no Pax Silica financing facility exists. We could only show none had been announced.
entries.supersedes: No Pax Silica financing facility, common fund or investment vehicle exists.
entries.summary: Checking the new funding notice against what this site already said turned up an overstatement of our own. The financing section asserted flatly that no Pax Silica financing facility, common fund or investment vehicle exists. We cannot show that. What we can show is that none has been announced on the record we search — the State Department's Pax Silica pages and releases, and the federal grants register — which is a different and smaller claim. The sentence is now scoped to those sources. The occasion for the correction is the notice's reference to a Pax Fund: we found no published authority, appropriation, size or governance document for it, and we are not treating our failure to find one as proof that no fund was constituted. A name in a synopsis is not a fund, and the absence of a document is not the absence of a thing. The underlying finding is unchanged and the verification pass expressly refused to let us weaken it — weakening a well-evidenced finding takes documents, and we have none.

entries.title: The hearing's own record: who said what about the population, and a peso figure we nearly got wrong
entries.supersedes: about 1,000 people associated with the Sitio Sapang Kawayan chieftain
entries.summary: Eric supplied the auto-generated transcript of the 14 August Senate hearing, which is the first time this report has had the proceeding itself rather than reporting about it. It changes two things we published this morning and adds a third. First, a correction: we attributed the figure of about 1,000 people to the chieftain of Sitio Sapang Kawayan. The recording does not establish who was speaking at that moment, so it is now attributed to a community witness describing the community's own census. Second, the 2013 date attached to BCDA's low count is restated as what a community witness said, not as established provenance — BCDA described its figure as houses seen on an earlier visit, not a census. Third, the transcript supplies the chain the news reports could not: NCIP told the committee it has no exact validated count, its 75-household figure came through a community source, and that figure covers one sitio inside the proposed area. A second affected group also surfaced — farmers, with two preliminary lists for a first phase of about 580 hectares, 182 in a figure associated with BCDA and 266 in the municipality's records, neither published. The verification pass refused all three of our drafts. Its most useful catch was arithmetic we had passed through without checking: the transcript rendered the assistance package as ₱300 per square metre and ₱300,000 per hectare, which cannot both be true, since a hectare is ten thousand square metres. Earlier records put it at ₱30 per square metre. We publish the ₱30 figure and not the other. Nothing here moves a key judgement; the question of displacement remains disputed, now on better evidence. And the transcript is machine speech recognition, not the official Senate record, which is why every figure above is qualified.

entries.title: How many indigenous people live on the site: three figures, no verified count
entries.summary: At the Senate hearing on 14 August, three different figures for the indigenous population of the proposed site were reportedly given in the same room: BCDA's, expressed in households; the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples' 75 households; and about 1,000 people, from the chieftain of Sitio Sapang Kawayan. It is tempting to report that as a three-way contradiction, and the first draft of this entry did. The adversarial verification pass refused it, for a reason worth stating plainly: the figures are not in the same units. Two count households, one counts people. Converted roughly, 75 households is about 285 people and 1,000 people is about 263 households — so the two larger figures are closer to each other than to BCDA's, and the real gap is between BCDA's estimate and NCIP's. The pass also refused to let this report say the chieftain's number is a count of the parcel, because nothing published establishes whether it describes the parcel, a community, or a wider claim area. What survives is narrower and, we think, more useful: no current, published, count of the site exists that reports households and people on the same date for a mapped area. Until one does, none of these numbers is a verified count of who lives there — and a categorical assurance that nobody will be displaced rests on the same missing document. The report's judgement on displacement is unchanged; a single hearing carried by one news organisation is not grounds to move it. Also corrected in the drafting: BCDA did not simply leave burial grounds undiscussed. It promised to respect them if affected, said the matter had not been discussed in detail, and proposed an inventory with NCIP.

entries.title: The United States' reply of 16 April enters the record
entries.summary: This report has always described the Philippine side's 9 April letter as a unilateral offer of land. It was one. What the report did not have was the American reply, and it has now been found — not in the news, but in a document published on the Board of Investments website, behind a page this monitor had already read and correctly judged to contain no news. The page's value was the documents it linked, and they are scans that no keyword search could see inside. The letter, dated 16 April 2026 and carrying Jacob S. Helberg's typed name beneath a blacked-out signature, records a conditional acceptance in principle: the United States accepts the two-year rent-free lease, but only subject to confirming the site and its boundaries and concluding an actual lease agreement, and it pushes funding, construction and operations into later arrangements that depend on US law and available funds. So the letter commits no American money, and nothing is concluded. Two honest limits travel with it. Its American authorship cannot be independently confirmed — the signature is redacted, and no State Department copy or archived version was found — and later statements from both governments show the framework still being negotiated. The adversarial verification pass refused three drafts of this entry before this wording, chiefly to stop the report saying the arrangement was 'no longer unilateral', which the record does not support. The same pass also corrected a reading of a second document: the AI Opportunity Partnership statement signed in Washington on 25 June is plurilateral, some 35 governments, not a further bilateral agreement, and it is carried here as context rather than as an instrument governing this project, because it contains no commitment specific to New Clark City.

entries.title: The Senate held its first committee hearing on the project
entries.supersedes: No committee action or institutional Senate position identified; the impact judgment does not move.
entries.summary: On 14 August 2026 the Senate Committee on Environment, Natural Resources and Climate Change, chaired by Sen. Raffy Tulfo, held a hearing on Pax Silica — the first committee hearing this monitor has identified. The stakeholder map's Senate row previously closed by recording that no committee action had been found. That is now superseded on its first limb and kept on its second: a hearing was held, and it canvassed the project's environmental, water, energy, displacement, land, sovereignty and mineral-processing issues, with Senate President Gatchalian calling it a "once-in-a-lifetime" opportunity while expressing conditional personal support — but no resolution, committee report or other institutional Senate position was identified as emerging from it. No key judgment, confidence level or scenario weight moves. Three adversarial gate passes refused successively narrower drafts before the published wording, which is the gate's own: it struck a claim that this was the first committee action outright (unprovable), and a list of conditions attributed to Gatchalian personally that the record placed with the hearing at large. A separate revision proposed for the same hearing — BCDA's testimony naming the Bangot/Bangat–O'Donnell and Abacan rivers as water sources — was refused twice and is not published, pending a transcript.

entries.title: Correction: the stakeholder exhibit still showed the old LGU finding, and miscounted the silent actors
entries.supersedes: Almost entirely absent from the public record: the largest gap in the evidence base — and, in the exhibit's introduction: “four actors central to whether this project can proceed have taken no institutional position on the record. One of them moved on 4 August: a first Senate resolution seeking an inquiry was filed, though the chamber itself has not acted.”
entries.summary: Two errors in exhibit 09, “who is loud, who is silent”. First, the correction published earlier today reached the report's text but not this chart: the Tarlac LGUs marker still described them as almost entirely absent from the public record, the exact sentence the correction retired. It now records what the record supports — Capas entered procedurally on 31 July with an information request and a subsequently reported meeting, no LGU has stated a position on the merits, and no independently verified Bamban or provincial position was found. The marker stays dashed, because a request for information is not a position. Second, and older: the introduction said four actors had taken no institutional position while the chart showed three. The NCIP left that group on 8 August, when a community dialogue was reported and its marker was un-dashed, but this sentence was not updated at the time. It now says three, names them, and says where the fourth went. No new claims were introduced: each fact here was verified when first published — the Capas entry earlier today, the Senate pushes on 12 and 13 August, the NCIP dialogue on 8 August.

entries.title: Correction: Tarlac local governments were not absent from the record
entries.supersedes: Almost entirely absent from the public record
entries.summary: This report said Tarlac's local governments were almost entirely absent from the public record, and called that the largest gap in the evidence. That was wrong, and had been since 31 July 2026. On that date the Inquirer reported that Capas Mayor Roseller “Boots” Rodriguez had written to the BCDA asking it to explain the project to the municipal government — its objectives, scope, timeline, environmental and social safeguards, expected benefits, regulatory compliance and local impacts.
